extracted.intended_audience: general readers of classic literature; students of Cervantes/Don Quixote
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Miguel de Cervantes' Don Quixote (chapters covering the lions episode, Don Diego de Miranda's house, poetical exchanges, and the lead-in to the Camacho–Quiteria wedding). Literary fiction in prose with comic and moralizing passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice of adventures
rubrics_metrics.description: A knight-errant should attempt adventures which encourage the hope of a successful issue, not those which entirely withhold it; for valour that trenches upon temerity savours rather of madness than of courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take on impossible enterprises that only expose you to foolhardiness; prefer exploits where there is at least a reasonable prospect of success. (Context/example: Don Quixote's decision to try and face lions, and the keeper's warning that such temerity borders on madness.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Valour as the mean between cowardice and temerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Valour is a virtue that occupies a place between two vicious extremes, cowardice and temerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is preferable for a valiant man to err toward rashness than to descend into cowardice: 'it will be a lesser evil for him who is valiant to rise till he reaches the point of rashness, than to sink until he reaches the point of cowardice.' (Author offers the analogy: easier for the prodigal than the miser to become generous.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties and virtues of a true knight-errant
rubrics_metrics.description: A true knight-errant must combine many learned and practical skills and moral virtues: he must be a jurist, a theologian, a physician (herbalist), an astronomer, know mathematics, be able to swim, shoe a horse, repair saddle and bridle; and morally be faithful to God and his lady, pure in thought, decorous in words, generous in works, valiant in deeds, patient in suffering, compassionate towards the needy, and an upholder of the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage enumerates both scholarly and hands-on proficiencies alongside cardinal and theological virtues—presenting knight-errantry as a comprehensive 'science' combining practical craft, learned knowledge, and moral excellence. Examples: know herbs to heal wounds in wastes and solitudes; be able to shoe a horse and repair tack; defend truth even at cost of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient demonstration of courage: challenge and await
rubrics_metrics.description: A brave champion is bound to do no more than challenge his enemy and wait for him on the field; if the adversary does not come, on him lies the disgrace, and he who waits carries off the crown of victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage may be shown by making the challenge and standing ready; failure of the foe to engage is the foe's dishonour. (Context/example: Don Quixote demands the keeper certify he opened the cage and that Don Quixote waited for the lions, treating that as proof of his valour.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Gloss-writing constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'laws of the gloss' are strict and limiting: they do not allow interrogations, nor 'said he,' nor 'I say,' nor turning verbs into nouns, or altering the construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glossing verse is presented as constrained by formal rules that can restrict expressive options; the gloss often cannot match the original text and may wander from its meaning. This functions as a brief critique of overly rigid literary forms and rules for poetic annotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where a knight shows to advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Different forms of knighthood display themselves best in different arenas: a court knight shows to advantage in tournaments, lists, and courtly entertainments; a knight-errant shows to greater advantage traversing deserts, solitudes, cross-roads, forests, and mountains in quest of perilous adventures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage contrasts public, ceremonial feats (tournaments, joustings) with the solitary, risky labours of an errant knight—arguing that the latter better prove the true calling and virtues of knight-errantry. Use this as a criterion for evaluating the appropriateness of knightly deeds and reputations.
